problem:
$$
a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,P=\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}{p}_{11} & {p}_{12} & {p}_{13} \\ {p}_{21} & {p}_{22} & {p}_{23} \\ {p}_{31} & {p}_{32} & {p}_{33}\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that the vector $a$ above spans ${S}^{⊥},$ and that $P$ is the orthogonal projection matrix of ${R}^{3}$ onto the subspace $S$, what is the value of ${p}_{22}+{p}_{31}?$

activity_context.topic_title: Projection Matrices, Linear Transformations and Their Properties

examples.knowledge_point: Finding an Orthogonal Projection Matrix Given Vectors That Span the Orthogonal Complement
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071876/assets/21268cd488766dc03da672cb931f1678644d2ada5629c90a591058d6f5954347.png)
Given that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ above spans $S^\perp,$ and that $P$ is the orthogonal projection matrix of $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto the subspace $S$, what is the value of $p_{13} + p_{32}?$
examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the orthogonal projection matrix onto $S^\perp = \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.$

Using the formula for the orthogonal projection matrix

$$
P_{S^\perp} = \mathbf{a} (\mathbf{a}^T\!\mathbf{a})^{-1} \mathbf{a}^T,
$$

we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={6}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $P_S  + P_{S^\perp} = I.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S} & =I-{P}_{{S}^{⊥}} \\  & =I-\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}5 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 5 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $p_{13} + p_{32} = (-2) + (-2) = -4.$

feedback.problem:
Which of the following are orthogonal projection matrices?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10} & -\frac{3}{10} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that $Q$ is an orthogonal projection matrix if and only if ${Q}^{2}=Q$ and ${Q}^{T}=Q.$ 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- $A$ is *not* an orthogonal projection matrix. We have
${A}^{T}=A$
but 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -5 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne A.\end{aligned}
$$

- $B$ is an orthogonal projection matrix. Indeed,
${B}^{T}=B$
and

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{2} & =B\cdot B \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10} & -\frac{3}{10} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10} & -\frac{3}{10} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{100}[\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{100}[\begin{aligned}90 & -30 \\ -30 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10} & -\frac{3}{10} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}] \\  & =B.\end{aligned}
$$

- $C$ is *not* an orthogonal projection matrix. We have
${C}^{T}=C$
but 

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & 4 \\ 4 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & \ne C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$B$ only."
